Lesson 1 — From a business problem to a research problem

Problem statement, sub-problems and research questions — the chain described by Leedy & Ormrod (2019, Chapter 2).

Slide 3 Lesson 1 — From a business problem to a research problem

Lecture notes

0:00–0:11

Opening and the Parking Lot (0:00–0:02)

Still on slideSlide 3 — Lesson 1 — From a business problem to a research problem

Good morning. Brick 1 was due last night at 23:59. You will get it back within a week, marked complete, partial or missing, with one comment. Before we start, the Parking Lot: the list of questions from last Friday that I promised to answer today.

Last week you met the client, Boréal Studio, and you started your 14-day time log. Today we do what a consultant does before anyone writes code: we decide exactly what we are trying to find out, what the software must do, how we will know that it is finished, where our evidence comes from, and what every column of our data means. That is why today is called the problem before the code.

From a complaint to a research problem (0:02–0:05)

Slide 4 From a complaint to a research problem

Leedy and Ormrod, the authors of our textbook, define research as a systematic process of collecting, analyzing and interpreting data in order to increase our understanding of a phenomenon. Every research project starts from a research problem: a question or a situation that can be resolved only by collecting data and interpreting it.

Here is what the owner of Boréal Studio wrote to us on Monday:

"Mornings disappear into the mailbox, the daily report is always late, and a vendor wants 20 $ per person per month for an assistant. Before I sign anything, I want to know what to automate first."

That is a complaint. It describes a difficulty, but it does not say what will be measured, what decision the answer will support, or how we will reach the answer. A problem statement turns the complaint into one short paragraph that names three things: the situation, the decision to be made, and the evidence that will be collected. For Boréal Studio:

Slide 5 The problem statement — situation, decision, evidence

"Boréal Studio, a five-person Montréal consultancy, spends a large part of every working day on six recurring routines. The owner must decide which routine to automate first, and whether a free assistant is sufficient or a paid tier at 20 $ per user per month is justified. This project measures how long each routine takes, prices that time at 28 $ per hour, builds a Python assistant that automates at least one routine, and compares the time it saves with the cost of each option, in order to recommend what to automate first."

That paragraph has 93 words; Brick 2 allows 150. Leedy and Ormrod give practical guidance for stating a problem: state it clearly and completely; make sure it is feasible with your time and resources (for us: fifteen Fridays, a team of two or three, and free tools); define the words that could be read in two ways; and keep an open mind, which means you do not write your conclusion into the problem.

Slide 6 What is not a research problem

They also list what is not a research problem. I paraphrase four cases: a task whose only purpose is to inform yourself ("learn about chatbots"); comparing two sets of data without interpreting the difference; computing a correlation only to show that one exists; and a question that can be answered with yes or no ("Is automation good?"). In each case, nothing has to be interpreted, so no new understanding is produced.

Sub-problems (0:05–0:08)

Slide 7 Sub-problems — four properties, three branches

Most research problems are too large to solve in one step, so the researcher divides them into sub-problems. Leedy and Ormrod describe four properties of good sub-problems. First, each sub-problem is a researchable unit by itself. Second, each one is tied to the interpretation of data. Third, together they add up to the whole problem, no more and no less. Fourth, there are few of them, usually between two and six.

Boréal Studio's problem divides naturally into three sub-problems, one per course we integrate:

  1. Microeconomics: what does each routine cost the studio per month, and what does each option (free assistant, paid tier, doing nothing) cost?
  2. Statistics: how long does each routine take, how much does that time vary, and did anything change after the report template (day 8) and the assistant pilot (day 10)?
  3. Python and OOP (Object-Oriented Programming): how can an assistant run a routine and measure the minutes it saves?

Be careful with a frequent mistake. Questions such as "Which chart library do we use?" or "How do we split the work in the team?" are pseudo-sub-problems: they are planning decisions. They must be made, but answering them does not require interpreting any data, so they do not belong in the problem tree.

Research questions (0:08–0:11)

Slide 8 Research questions (1/2) — the course template

A research question is a sub-problem written as an open question that the data and the methods of the project can answer. The course template, which you will refine in Brick 2, is:

  • RQ1 (Research Question 1), the Statistics question: Which routines cost the most time, and which are the most variable?
  • RQ2 (Research Question 2), the Microeconomics question: What is an hour of staff time worth, what does automation cost, and where is the break-even between the free tier and a paid assistant?
  • RQ3 (Research Question 3), the integration question: Which routines should JARVIS automate first, how much time does it save, and what is the risk?
Slide 9 Research questions (2/2) — four checks before you accept one

Before you accept a research question, apply four checks. One: it is a question, and an open one, so it cannot be answered by yes or no. Two: it names something measurable in our data or in the three given numbers: minutes, interruptions, runs, dollars. Three: it belongs to one sub-problem. Four: it can be answered with your data by January 22. "How can the studio become more productive?" fails check two: the word productive has no unit in our data. "Is automation good?" fails checks one and two.

Why spend ten minutes on this? Because in January the Results section of your report and your conclusions must answer these research questions, and nothing else. A vague research question written today produces a vague conclusion in January. The Mid-Term also asks it directly: Part B gives you a new small-business scenario and asks for a problem, one sub-problem and one research question.

Key terms of this lesson

TermScientific explanation
ResearchA systematic process of collecting, analyzing and interpreting data to increase understanding of a phenomenon (Leedy & Ormrod, 2019).
Research problemA question or situation that can be resolved only by collecting and interpreting data; the starting point of a research project.
Problem statementA short paragraph (at most 150 words in Brick 2) that names the situation, the decision to be supported and the evidence that will be collected.
Sub-problemA researchable part of the main problem; the sub-problems together add up to the whole problem and are few (two to six).
Pseudo-sub-problemA planning or procedural decision (for example, which chart library to use) that does not require interpreting data.
Research question (RQ)A sub-problem written as an open question that names something measurable and can be answered with the project's data and methods.

Real-life example

Slide 11 Real-life example — the owner's e-mail becomes a problem tree

Real-life example — The owner's e-mail becomes a problem tree

Task of the example. Turn the owner's Monday e-mail into (a) a problem statement of at most 150 words, (b) three sub-problems, one per course, (c) research questions checked with the four rules, and (d) a map that says which data and which method answer each research question.

How it relates to this lesson. This is Lesson 1 applied end to end: complaint → problem statement → sub-problems → research questions (Leedy & Ormrod, 2019, Chapter 2). The demo below runs the four checks on five candidate questions; the figure shows the finished tree.

The situation. On Monday morning the owner sends three sentences: mornings disappear into the mailbox, the daily report is always late, and a vendor offers an assistant at 20 $ per person per month. A team of three students reads it on Friday and works in this order.

  1. Problem statement. They write the 93-word paragraph shown in the script and check it against Leedy and Ormrod's guidance: clear and complete, feasible in fifteen Fridays, terms defined (a routine, a run, the paid tier), no conclusion written in advance.
  2. Sub-problems. They split the problem into three parts (cost for Microeconomics, time and variability for Statistics, automation and measurement for Python) and verify that together they cover the owner's question and nothing else.
  3. Research questions. They draft five candidate questions. Three pass the four checks and become RQ1 (Research Question 1), RQ2 (Research Question 2) and RQ3 (Research Question 3); two are rejected: "Is automation good for the studio?" (a yes/no question with nothing measurable) and "How can the studio become more productive?" (nothing measurable).
  4. Data map. For each accepted question they write the columns and the method that will answer it:
Research question Data that answers it Method Answered in
RQ1 (Research Question 1) — which routines take the most minutes, which vary the most routine, minutes, staff_id, date mean, median, SD (standard deviation) per routine Brick 4 (Oct 22)
RQ2 (Research Question 2) — monthly cost, break-even of the 20 $ paid tier minutes, routine + 28 $/h, 20 $/user/month, the free quota cost per month, break-even hours Brick 3 (Oct 15)
RQ3 (Research Question 3) — what to automate first, minutes saved, risk tool (manual / template / jarvis), minutes, date (before/after day 10) before/after comparison, recommendation pattern Brick 7 (Nov 12), Brick 11 (Dec 17)

Where these deliverables go next. The problem statement and RQ1 (Research Question 1)–RQ3 (Research Question 3) are the first part of Brick 2 (docs/requirements.md, due October 8) and become section 1, Introduction & Problem, of your technical report. Brick 3 answers RQ2 (Research Question 2) with numbers, Brick 4 answers RQ1, Brick 7 gives the first answer to RQ3, and in Sprint 2 (Brick 11) every research question must be answered with a number and a table. Part B of the Mid-Term (November 20) asks you to do steps 1 to 3 for a new scenario.

Demo 1 — Problem tree and research-question checker

Task of the code. Build the problem tree of Boréal Studio (problem → three sub-problems → candidate research questions), apply four explicit rules to each candidate, keep the ones that pass, and check that the accepted questions cover every sub-problem and stay few in number.

How it relates to the lecture. Lesson 1: the chain research problem → sub-problems → research questions, and the properties of good sub-problems (Leedy & Ormrod, 2019, Chapter 2). The accepted questions are the RQ1 (Research Question 1)–RQ3 (Research Question 3) that Brick 2 asks for.

The steps below are the real execution of demo1_problem_tree.py, recorded statement by statement with Python 3. Keyboard: space = start/pause, ← → = one step.

  1. 1# =====================================================================
  2. 2# DEMO 1 - FROM THE OWNER'S QUESTION TO RESEARCH QUESTIONS
  3. 3# CS (Computer Science) 251 - Integrative Project 1 - Class 2, Lesson 1
  4. 4#
  5. 5# TASK OF THIS CODE: build the problem tree of Boréal Studio
  6. 6# (problem -> sub-problems -> research questions) and test every
  7. 7# candidate research question with four explicit rules adapted from
  8. 8# Leedy & Ormrod (2019, Chapter 2). The program prints a verdict for
  9. 9# each candidate and checks that the accepted questions cover every
  10. 10# sub-problem.
  11. 11#
  12. 12# HOW IT RELATES TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 1 teaches the chain
  13. 13# research problem -> sub-problems -> research questions. The accepted
  14. 14# questions are the RQ1-RQ3 (Research Questions 1 to 3) that Brick 2
  15. 15# asks for; Bricks 3, 4, 7 and 11 answer them with numbers.

  20. 20# Acceptable Use Policy (v2.0):
  21. 21# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
  22. 22# =====================================================================
  23. 23
  24. 24# The owner's question, rewritten as the research problem: the root of the tree
  25. 25problem = "Which routine should Boréal Studio automate first, and is a free assistant good enough?"
  26. 26
  27. 27# The three sub-problems; each key is the course whose methods solve that part
  28. 28sub_problems = {
  29. 29 # Microeconomics prices the time and the options
  30. 30 "Micro": "What does each routine cost per month, and what does each option cost?",
  31. 31 # Statistics describes what the time log shows
  32. 32 "Stats": "How long does each routine take, and how much does that time vary?",
  33. 33 # Python builds the assistant and measures what it saves
  34. 34 "Python": "How can an assistant run a routine and measure the minutes it saves?",
  35. 35# This closing brace ends the dictionary of sub-problems
  36. 36}
  37. 37
  38. 38# Words that show a question names something measurable in our data or in the given numbers
  39. 39MEASURABLE = ("minutes", "cost", "$", "hours", "interruptions", "runs")
  40. 40
  41. 41# Openings that turn a sentence into a yes/no question
  42. 42YES_NO_STARTS = ("is ", "are ", "does ", "do ", "can ", "should ", "will ")
  43. 43
  44. 44# Candidate research questions drafted by a team: (label, sub-problem, text)
  45. 45candidates = [
  46. 46 # A question about time: it names minutes and asks about variation (Statistics)
  47. 47 ("RQ1", "Stats", "Which routines take the most minutes per run, and which vary the most?"),
  48. 48 # A question about money: it names the cost, the hourly value and the paid tier (Microeconomics)
  49. 49 ("RQ2", "Micro", "What does each routine cost per month at 28 $/h, and how many saved hours make a 20 $ paid tier worth it?"),
  50. 50 # A question about automation: it names the minutes saved (Python)
  51. 51 ("RQ3", "Python", "Which routine should JARVIS automate first, and how many minutes per run does it save?"),
  52. 52 # A yes/no question: it names nothing we can measure
  53. 53 ("RQ4", "Python", "Is automation good for the studio?"),
  54. 54 # A vague question: 'productive' has no unit in our data
  55. 55 ("RQ5", "Micro", "How can the studio become more productive?"),
  56. 56# This closing bracket ends the list of candidates
  57. 57]
  58. 58
  59. 59
  60. 60# Define the function that applies the four rules to one candidate question
  61. 61def check(course, question):
  62. 62 # Work on a lowercase copy so that "Minutes" and "minutes" are treated the same
  63. 63 text = question.lower()
  64. 64 # Rule 1: the sentence is written as a question (it ends with a question mark)
  65. 65 is_question = question.endswith("?")
  66. 66 # Rule 2: the question names at least one measurable quantity from our data
  67. 67 measurable = any(word in text for word in MEASURABLE)
  68. 68 # Rule 3: the question is open; a yes/no question cannot guide data collection
  69. 69 open_question = not text.startswith(YES_NO_STARTS)
  70. 70 # Rule 4: the question belongs to one of our sub-problems (one course)
  71. 71 tied = course in sub_problems
  72. 72 # Send back the four results, in the order of the rules
  73. 73 return {"question": is_question, "measurable": measurable, "open": open_question, "sub-problem": tied}
  74. 74
  75. 75
  76. 76# Print the research problem first, as the root of the tree
  77. 77print("PROBLEM:", problem)
  78. 78
  79. 79# Start with an empty list of accepted research questions
  80. 80accepted = []
  81. 81
  82. 82# Start with an empty dictionary that keeps the verdict of every candidate
  83. 83verdicts = {}
  84. 84
  85. 85# Examine the candidates one at a time
  86. 86for rq_id, course, question in candidates:
  87. 87 # Apply the four rules to this candidate
  88. 88 result = check(course, question)
  89. 89 # The candidate passes only if every rule is true
  90. 90 passed = all(result.values())
  91. 91 # Store the detailed result so it can be shown and discussed
  92. 92 verdicts[rq_id] = result
  93. 93 # Keep the candidate when it passed all four rules
  94. 94 if passed:
  95. 95 # Add it to the list of accepted research questions
  96. 96 accepted.append((rq_id, course, question))
  97. 97 # Print one line per candidate: label, sub-problem, verdict, text
  98. 98 print(f"{rq_id} [{course}] {'ACCEPT' if passed else 'REJECT'}: {question}")
  99. 99
  100. 100# Collect the sub-problems covered by the accepted questions (a set has no duplicates)
  101. 101covered = {course for _, course, _ in accepted}
  102. 102
  103. 103# Leedy & Ormrod: together the sub-problems must add up to the whole problem
  104. 104adds_up = covered == set(sub_problems)
  105. 105
  106. 106# Leedy & Ormrod: the number of sub-problems stays small - between two and six
  107. 107small = 2 <= len(accepted) <= 6
  108. 108
  109. 109# Print the summary that goes into the problem statement of Brick 2
  110. 110print(f"Accepted: {len(accepted)} | every sub-problem covered: {adds_up} | small number: {small}")
  111. 111

Execution log — every step that has run (click a line to return to it)
    

    How the code works — step by step
    1. Press Start. The first statements store the research problem and the three sub-problems; in the visualization the root box and the three course branches appear.
    2. The tuples MEASURABLE and YES_NO_STARTS hold the words used by rules 2 and 3. Watch the Variables panel: every new name appears there as soon as its statement has run.
    3. The list candidates is built in one step: five questions, each with a label and the sub-problem it claims to belong to. Five grey leaves appear under their branches.
    4. def check(...) only defines the function; nothing is checked yet. The function runs later, each time the loop calls it.
    5. The for loop takes the first candidate. The step calls check() moves the execution into the function: the Execution log shows the call, and the panel Locals of check() shows the arguments course and question.
    6. Inside check() each rule is one statement: is_question, measurable, open_question, tied. The four rule lamps under the tree turn green (true) or red (false) one by one.
    7. return sends the dictionary of four results back to the loop; the log shows the returned value. passed = all(...) is true only if the four results are true; the leaf turns green (accepted) or red (rejected).
    8. RQ4 (Research Question 4), "Is automation good for the studio?", fails rule 3 because it starts with is, and rule 2 because it names nothing measurable. RQ5 (Research Question 5) fails rule 2 only.
    9. After the loop, a set comprehension collects the sub-problems covered by the accepted questions. adds_up compares that set with the three sub-problems (Leedy and Ormrod's add up to the whole); small checks the number is between two and six.
    10. Press Pause at any moment: everything stays on screen, and Start resumes from the same statement. Next step and Back move one statement at a time; clicking a line in the execution log jumps to that step. Restart returns to the beginning.

    Slide 14 Lesson 2 — Requirements analysis
    Lecture notes
    0:15–0:26
    What a requirement is (0:15–0:17)
    Slide 15 What a requirement is
    

    A requirement is a statement of something a system must do, or of a property it must have, written so that someone can check whether the delivered system satisfies it. Requirements analysis is the work of discovering, writing, classifying, checking and agreeing on requirements with the stakeholders, the people who use the system or are affected by it. For JARVIS the stakeholders are the owner, the staff, and, in this course, the people who assess the Product Defense in January.
    

    The international standard for this work is ISO/IEC/IEEE (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission / Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers) 29148:2018, Requirements engineering. It lists the characteristics of a well-formed requirement: necessary, appropriate, unambiguous, complete, singular, feasible, verifiable, correct and conforming. Today we use three of them. Unambiguous: the statement can be read in only one way. Singular: one requirement per statement. Verifiable: a test, an inspection or a measurement can prove that it is met. The same standard fixes a convention you will use in Brick 2: "shall" marks a binding requirement; "should" marks a goal or a wish.
    

    Functional and non-functional requirements (0:17–0:20)
    Slide 16 Functional versus non-functional requirements
    

    A functional requirement (FR) describes a behaviour: given an input or an event, the system produces an output or changes its data. Two examples from our schedule: "The assistant shall log a routine from one command." "The assistant shall compute the break-even hours for the paid tier."
    

    A non-functional requirement (NFR) describes a quality of the system or a constraint on how it performs its functions. The quality model ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization / International Electrotechnical Commission) 25010:2023 groups these qualities into nine characteristics; four of them matter to us: performance efficiency, reliability, security and maintainability. JARVIS has four non-functional requirements written into the course:
    

      

    • it runs from a fresh clone of the repository in under 2 minutes;
      • 

    • it works with no API (Application Programming Interface) key and no network (the offline rule from Class 1);
      • 

    • it never crashes on an empty cell: a bad row is skipped and counted;
      • 

    • the database file data/jarvis.db stays under 1 MB (megabyte).
      • 

    

    A simple test separates the two types. A functional requirement answers what does it do? A non-functional requirement answers how well, or under which limits?
    

    A non-functional requirement without a number or a checkable condition cannot be verified. "JARVIS shall be fast" is not a requirement yet. "JARVIS shall answer a log command in under one second on the lab computer" is one: a stopwatch can decide.
    

    User stories (0:20–0:23)
    Slide 17 User stories — As a…, I want…, so that…
    

    A user story describes one requirement from the point of view of the person who benefits from it, in one sentence: "As a role, I want goal, so that benefit." The Agile Alliance dates this role–feature–benefit template to 2001. Brick 2 asks for five stories with at least three kinds of role:
    

      

    • As the owner, I want a monthly cost for each routine, so that I can decide what to automate first.
      • 

    • As a staff member, I want to log a routine with one command, so that recording my time takes seconds.
      • 

    • As JARVIS with no API (Application Programming Interface) key, I want to understand requests with rules, so that the assistant still works offline.
      • 

    

    The third story has an unusual role, the system itself in a degraded condition, because the offline rule is one of the most important requirements of the project, and it deserves its own story.
    

    A common checklist for stories, introduced by Bill Wake in 2003, is INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable): a good story has all six of these properties. Today the last letter, T for Testable, matters most.
    

    Acceptance criteria (0:23–0:26)
    Slide 18 Acceptance criteria — Given, When, Then
    

    Acceptance criteria are the conditions a story must satisfy to be accepted as finished. A widely used format comes from BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) and is supported by tools such as Cucumber's Gherkin language: Given the starting situation, When an action happens, Then an observable result follows. For the staff member's story:
    

      

    • Given an empty log, when I type log 25 min email_triage, then one entry is stored with routine email_triage and minutes 25.
      • 

    • Given an empty log, when I type log twenty min email_triage, then nothing is stored and JARVIS replies with the expected format.
      • 

    

    Each criterion becomes one automated test: in Class 10 you will write exactly these as pytest tests. Two rules to remember: a story without acceptance criteria can never be declared finished, and a non-functional requirement without a threshold can never be tested.
    Key terms of this lesson
    TermScientific explanation
    RequirementA statement of something a system must do, or a property it must have, written so that it can be checked.
    StakeholderA person who uses the system or is affected by it: the owner, the staff, and the assessors of the Product Defense.
    Functional requirement (FR)A behaviour: given an input or event, the system produces an output or changes its data.
    Non-functional requirement (NFR)A quality or a constraint on how the system performs its functions (speed, reliability, size, availability without network...).
    VerifiableA test, an inspection or a measurement can prove that the requirement is met; vague adjectives need a threshold.
    User storyOne requirement from the point of view of the person who benefits: As a role, I want goal, so that benefit.
    Acceptance criteriaThe conditions a story must satisfy to be accepted as finished, often written Given / When / Then.

From six statements collected in a 20-minute interview with the owner and one staff member, classify each statement as functional or non-functional, flag the statement that cannot be tested, write the staff member's user story, express its acceptance criteria as Given / When / Then, and run the two criteria against a six-line prototype of the log command.

The demo performs every step with real Python code; the figure shows the resulting requirements map.

    What the team does. It labels statements 1 and 2 as functional, FR1 (Functional Requirement 1) and FR2 (Functional Requirement 2), and statements 3 to 6 as non-functional, NFR3 (Non-Functional Requirement 3) to NFR6 (Non-Functional Requirement 6). Statement 6 is flagged: fast and easy have no threshold, and should marks a wish. The team rewrites it in Brick 2 as two verifiable NFRs (Non-Functional Requirements): "JARVIS shall answer a log command in under one second on the lab computer" and "A new user shall log a first routine within 5 minutes, using only the README." Then it writes the staff member's story and two acceptance criteria, and runs them against a prototype of the command: a correct request stores one row; a request with the minutes written in words stores nothing and explains the expected format.
    

    Where these deliverables go next.
    

      

    • The requirements list with its FR (Functional Requirement)/NFR labels and the five user stories with acceptance criteria are deliverables of Brick 2 and become section 2, Requirements, of the report. The Final rubric (Methodology, Exemplary level) asks for requirements exhaustively mapped to the solution.
      • 

    • The prototype is the first version of the OfflineProvider of Brick 7: a regular expression that turns log 25 min email_triage into an intent.
      • 

    • The acceptance criteria become pytest tests in Brick 9 (at least six tests) and Brick 10, which adds three bad-input cases and demonstrates the offline fallback; that demonstration is the evidence for NFR4 (Non-Functional Requirement 4).
      • 

    • NFR3 (Non-Functional Requirement 3), a fresh clone that runs in under 2 minutes, is checked at the dress rehearsal (Class 14) and during the Product Defense.
      •

    Demo 2 — Requirements classifier and acceptance checks
    Task of the code. Classify six interview statements as FR (Functional Requirement) or NFR (Non-Functional Requirement) with explicit word lists, flag the statements that cannot be tested, print the user story of the staff member, and run its two Given/When/Then acceptance criteria against a six-line prototype of the log command.
    How it relates to the lecture. Lesson 2: functional versus non-functional requirements, verifiable wording, user stories and acceptance criteria. The classification rules are a first pass that a person confirms; the prototype is the first version of the OfflineProvider (Brick 7) and the criteria are the first version of the pytest tests (Bricks 9–10).
    
  
    The steps below are the real execution of demo2_requirements.py, recorded statement by statement with Python 3. Keyboard: space = start/pause, ← → = one step.
    
 
    
  
  
  
  
 
    
 
    
  
    1. 1# =====================================================================
    2. 2# DEMO 2 - FROM AN INTERVIEW TO TESTED REQUIREMENTS
    3. 3# CS (Computer Science) 251 - Integrative Project 1 - Class 2, Lesson 2
    4. 4#
    5. 5# TASK OF THIS CODE: take six statements collected in a short interview
    6. 6# with the owner and one staff member, classify each one as a functional
    7. 7# requirement (FR - what the system does) or a non-functional requirement
    8. 8# (NFR - how well or under which limits it does it), flag the ones that
    9. 9# cannot be tested, write the staff member's user story, and run its two
    10. 10# acceptance criteria (Given / When / Then) against a six-line prototype
    11. 11# of the "log" command.
    12. 12#
    13. 13# HOW IT RELATES TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 2 - requirements analysis:
    14. 14# FR versus NFR, verifiable wording, user stories and acceptance
    15. 15# criteria. The requirements and stories go into Brick 2; the prototype
    16. 16# becomes the OfflineProvider of Brick 7; the acceptance criteria become
    17. 17# pytest tests in Bricks 9 and 10.
    18. 18#
    19. 19# Standard library only - runs with Python 3.12 or newer.
    20. 20# Educational material - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub (c) 2026.
    21. 21# Use is subject to the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and
    22. 22# Acceptable Use Policy (v2.0):
    23. 23# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
    24. 24# =====================================================================
    25. 25 
    26. 26# Import the standard module for regular expressions (patterns that match text)
    27. 27import re
    28. 28 
    29. 29# The six statements written down during the interview, in the order they were said
    30. 30statements = [
    31. 31    # Said by the staff member: an action the assistant performs
    32. 32    "JARVIS shall record a routine run from one command, such as 'log 25 min email_triage'.",
    33. 33    # Said by the owner: a computation the assistant performs
    34. 34    "JARVIS shall compute the monthly cost of each routine at 28 $/h.",
    35. 35    # Said by the instructor: a limit on installation time
    36. 36    "JARVIS shall run from a fresh clone in under 2 minutes.",
    37. 37    # Said by the owner: a condition the assistant must survive
    38. 38    "JARVIS shall work with no API key and no network.",
    39. 39    # Said by the instructor: a limit on the size of a file
    40. 40    "The database file shall stay under 1 MB.",
    41. 41    # Said by the staff member: a wish with no threshold
    42. 42    "JARVIS should be fast and easy to use.",
    43. 43# This closing bracket ends the list of statements
    44. 44]
    45. 45 
    46. 46# Words that signal a quality or a limit (non-functional) rather than a behaviour
    47. 47QUALITY_WORDS = ("under", "within", "no api key", "no network", "fast", "easy", "stay")
    48. 48 
    49. 49# Adjectives that make a statement impossible to test until a number replaces them
    50. 50VAGUE_WORDS = ("fast", "easy", "smart", "user-friendly", "better")
    51. 51 
    52. 52# A pattern that finds a number followed by a unit, for example "2 minutes" or "1 MB"
    53. 53THRESHOLD = re.compile(r"\d+\s*(minutes|min|seconds|mb)\b")
    54. 54 
    55. 55# Verbs that describe an observable output of a function
    56. 56OUTPUT_VERBS = ("record", "compute", "list", "show", "export")
    57. 57 
    58. 58 
    59. 59# Define the function that classifies one statement and checks if it can be tested
    60. 60def analyse(text):
    61. 61    # Work on a lowercase copy so the word lists match whatever the capitals
    62. 62    low = text.lower()
    63. 63    # Non-functional if any quality word appears; otherwise functional
    64. 64    kind = "NFR" if any(word in low for word in QUALITY_WORDS) else "FR"
    65. 65    # A statement that relies on a vague adjective can never be verified
    66. 66    vague = any(word in low for word in VAGUE_WORDS)
    67. 67    # A functional requirement is testable when it names an observable output
    68. 68    if kind == "FR":
    69. 69        # Look for one of the output verbs
    70. 70        testable = any(verb in low for verb in OUTPUT_VERBS)
    71. 71    # A non-functional requirement is testable when it has a threshold or a yes/no condition
    72. 72    else:
    73. 73        # A number with a unit, or the binary condition "no API key"
    74. 74        testable = (THRESHOLD.search(low) is not None or "no api key" in low) and not vague
    75. 75    # Send back the type and the testability verdict
    76. 76    return kind, testable
    77. 77 
    78. 78 
    79. 79# Start an empty list that will hold the analysed requirements
    80. 80requirements = []
    81. 81 
    82. 82# Analyse the statements one at a time, numbering them from 1
    83. 83for number, text in enumerate(statements, start=1):
    84. 84    # Classify the statement and check whether it can be tested
    85. 85    kind, testable = analyse(text)
    86. 86    # Build an identifier such as FR1 or NFR3 from the type and the number
    87. 87    req_id = f"{kind}{number}"
    88. 88    # Store the result as a small dictionary (one row of the requirements register)
    89. 89    requirements.append({"id": req_id, "type": kind, "testable": testable, "text": text})
    90. 90    # Print the row so the team can review it
    91. 91    print(f"{req_id:<5} {'testable' if testable else 'NOT TESTABLE - add a threshold'} | {text}")
    92. 92 
    93. 93# The staff member's user story for the first statement, in the template As a / I want / so that
    94. 94story = {"role": "a staff member", "goal": "log a routine with one command", "benefit": "recording my time takes seconds"}
    95. 95 
    96. 96# Print the user story as one sentence
    97. 97print(f"STORY: As {story['role']}, I want to {story['goal']}, so that {story['benefit']}.")
    98. 98 
    99. 99# The acceptance criteria of the story: (Given, When, Then = number of rows expected in the log)
    100. 100criteria = [
    101. 101    # Criterion 1: a correct command stores exactly one row
    102. 102    ("an empty log", "log 25 min email_triage", 1),
    103. 103    # Criterion 2: a command with the minutes in words stores nothing and explains the format
    104. 104    ("an empty log", "log twenty min email_triage", 0),
    105. 105# This closing bracket ends the list of criteria
    106. 106]
    107. 107 
    108. 108# The rule of the prototype: the word log, a number, the word min, a routine name
    109. 109PATTERN = re.compile(r"log\s+(\d+)\s*min\s+(\w+)")
    110. 110 
    111. 111 
    112. 112# Define the prototype of the log command (it becomes the OfflineProvider in Brick 7)
    113. 113def log_time(text, log):
    114. 114    # Try to match the whole request against the pattern
    115. 115    match = PATTERN.fullmatch(text.strip())
    116. 116    # If the request does not follow the pattern, store nothing and explain the expected format
    117. 117    if match is None:
    118. 118        # The reply tells the user what JARVIS expected
    119. 119        return "Sorry - write it as: log <minutes> min <routine>"
    120. 120    # Otherwise store one row with the routine name and the minutes as an integer
    121. 121    log.append({"routine": match.group(2), "minutes": int(match.group(1))})
    122. 122    # Confirm to the user what was stored
    123. 123    return f"Logged {match.group(1)} min of {match.group(2)}."
    124. 124 
    125. 125 
    126. 126# Start an empty list for the results of the acceptance checks
    127. 127results = []
    128. 128 
    129. 129# Run every acceptance criterion as a small test
    130. 130for given, when, expected_rows in criteria:
    131. 131    # Given: start from an empty log
    132. 132    log = []
    133. 133    # When: send the request to the prototype
    134. 134    reply = log_time(when, log)
    135. 135    # Then: the number of stored rows must equal the expected number
    136. 136    passed = len(log) == expected_rows
    137. 137    # Keep the outcome for the report and the visualization
    138. 138    results.append({"when": when, "reply": reply, "rows": len(log), "passed": passed})
    139. 139    # Print the criterion in Given / When / Then form with its result
    140. 140    print(f"GIVEN {given} WHEN '{when}' THEN rows={len(log)} (expected {expected_rows}) -> {'PASS' if passed else 'FAIL'}")
    141. 141

    Execution log — every step that has run (click a line to return to it)
      

      How the code works — step by step
      1. Press Start. import re loads the regular-expression module; the list statements is built in one step and six grey cards appear in the Interview notes column.
      2. QUALITY_WORDS, VAGUE_WORDS, THRESHOLD and OUTPUT_VERBS are the rules of the analysis. They are visible in the Variables panel: a rule you can read is a rule you can discuss and correct.
      3. def analyse(...) defines the function. The loop then takes statement 1 and calls analyse(): the Locals of analyse() panel shows text, then low, kind, vague and testable as each statement runs.
      4. Statement 1 contains none of the quality words, so kind becomes "FR"; it contains the verb record, so testable is true. The card moves to the Functional column with a green testable badge.
      5. Statement 3 contains under and the threshold 2 minutes, so it becomes NFR3 (Non-Functional Requirement 3), testable. Statement 4 has no number but has the binary condition no API (Application Programming Interface) key, which a test can create by removing the key.
      6. Statement 6 contains fast and easy: it is non-functional, and vague is true, so testable is false. Its card gets a red add a threshold badge — the classic NFR (Non-Functional Requirement) that must be rewritten.
      7. After the loop, the user story is printed in the template As a / I want / so that, and the two acceptance criteria are stored as (Given, When, expected rows).
      8. log_time() is the prototype: PATTERN.fullmatch() either matches the whole request or returns None. In the second criterion the minutes are written in words, the pattern does not match, and the function returns the help message without storing anything.
      9. Each criterion is executed as a small test: Given an empty log, When the request is sent, Then the number of stored rows must equal the expected number. Both lamps of the Acceptance tests panel turn green: PASS.
      10. Use Pause, Next step, Back and the clickable Execution log to discuss any step; Restart clears everything.

      Lesson 3 · Part 3Scope, SMART objectives and project selection0:30–0:41 · then fun quiz + zen break
      Lesson 3 — Scope, SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives and project selection
      What the project will and will not do, what it assumes, what limits it, what it commits to — and which data it may use.
      Slide 23 Lesson 3 — Scope, SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives and project selection
      Lecture notes
      0:30–0:41
      Scope and delimitations (0:30–0:33)
      Slide 24 Scope and delimitations
      

      The scope of a project is the set of results it will deliver: features, documents and data. The PMI (Project Management Institute), the professional association that publishes the PMBOK (Project Management Body of Knowledge) Guide, treats scope as the work needed to deliver those results, and no more. Leedy and Ormrod add a word that every research proposal needs: the delimitations of the study, an explicit list of what the researcher will not do. Writing both lists prevents the most common failure of student projects, scope creep: features added every week until nothing works on the day of the defense.
      

      For JARVIS, the scope is: the six routines of Boréal Studio; the 14-day time log; the statistics and economics engines; the offline provider plus one free API (Application Programming Interface) tier; the tiny SQLite database; a dashboard with aggregated numbers; the report and the defense.
      

      The delimitations, that is, what JARVIS will not do: voice commands; reading real mailboxes or real calendars; a mobile application; any paid service; any data about real people other than the team's own anonymised logs.
      

      Assumptions and constraints (0:33–0:35)
      Slide 25 Assumptions and constraints
      

      An assumption is a statement the team treats as true for planning, without proof. It must be written down, because if it turns out to be false the results change. Our assumptions: 28 $ per hour is a fair loaded cost for the studio; the fourteen logged days are typical working days; the staff logged their minutes honestly; the minutes saved in the pilot from day 10 will continue after the pilot.
      

      A constraint is a limit that the project cannot change. Ours: fifteen Fridays and a Product Defense on January 22, 2027; teams of two or three; Python only; free API (Application Programming Interface) tiers whose quotas change over time (you will record the number and the date you read it); no personal data in any public repository; a database file under 1 MB (megabyte).
      

      The difference matters later. Assumptions are tested and discussed: in Sprint 2 your recommendation must list its risks and assumptions. Constraints are respected: every objective you write must fit inside them.
      

      SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives (0:35–0:39)
      Slide 26 SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives — and the January test
      

      An objective is a result the team commits to deliver by a date. The best-known test for objectives is SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound), first published by George T. Doran in 1981 in Management Review. Doran's own letters were Specific, Measurable, Assignable, Realistic and Time-related; later authors changed some of them, and this course uses the most common modern set:
      

        

      • Specific: it names exactly what will be delivered;
        • 

      • Measurable: it states a number or an observable test of success;
        • 

      • Achievable: it fits the team's hours and the tools the course allows;
        • 

      • Relevant: it serves one of the research questions;
        • 

      • Time-bound: it has a date.
        • 

      

      Two examples from our schedule. "Make JARVIS smart" satisfies none of the five letters: no deliverable, no measure, no estimate, no research question, no date. "Log 14 days of routines and compute the SD (standard deviation) of minutes per routine by October 22" satisfies all five, and October 22 is exactly the due date of Brick 4.
      

      For this course, add one more check, the January test: for every objective, ask can we demonstrate this at the Product Defense on January 22? If the answer is no, the objective is outside the scope or it must become smaller. Three tools that work are worth more than ten tools that do not.
      

      Selecting and confirming the project (0:39–0:41)
      Slide 27 Selecting and confirming the project
      

      Every team works on the same business problem. The default data set is boreal_routines_2026.csv: synthetic, already anonymised, and identical for everyone, so the grading is comparable. A team may propose its own real small-business or team data instead, under three conditions, all of them required:
      

        

      1. the data is anonymised: no names, no message contents, only routine names, minutes and timestamps;
        2. 

      2. the organization gives written permission: section 7.9 of the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy applies to any work involving a real organization, and it also says that a relative who owns the business is not automatically the person entitled to give it;
        3. 

      3. the instructor approves it, today in the workshop or at the latest with Brick 2.
        4. 

      

      If any condition is missing, you use the default data set. The rubric is the same in both cases.
      Key terms of this lesson
      TermScientific explanation
      ScopeThe set of results the project will deliver — features, documents and data — and the work needed to deliver them.
      DelimitationAn explicit statement of what the project or study will not do (Leedy & Ormrod).
      Scope creepThe uncontrolled growth of a project's scope after it has started, usually by adding features week after week.
      AssumptionA statement treated as true for planning without proof; it must be written down and later tested or discussed.
      ConstraintA limit the project cannot change: dates, team size, allowed tools, quotas, privacy rules.
      ObjectiveA result the team commits to deliver by a date.
      SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound)Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound — the five tests of a well-written objective (after Doran, 1981).
      January testThe course check for every objective: can it be demonstrated at the Product Defense on January 22, 2027?
      Slide 28 Activity — fun quiz, then a zen break
      Fun quiz + zen break · 0:41–0:45
      Fun quiz, then zen break (0:41–0:45). Four questions, hands up: (1) Is "make JARVIS smart" SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound)? (2) Is "log 14 days of routines and compute the SD (standard deviation) of minutes per routine by October 22" SMART? (3) Which letter fails in "connect JARVIS to voice, calendar and e-mail by December 18"? (4) "The free API (Application Programming Interface) quota will not change before January": assumption or constraint?
      

      Then two minutes of zen break: stand up, roll your shoulders backwards five times, breathe in for four seconds, hold for four, breathe out for four. Repeat three times.

      Capacity. Three members × 4 hours per week (2 h in the workshop, 2 h at home) = 12 hours per week. Before October 22 the team has 2 full weeks (24 h); before November 6, 5 weeks (60 h); before December 18, 11 weeks (132 h).
      

      Result. Objectives 2, 3 and 5 are SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound). Objective 1 fails all five letters. Objective 4 fails Achievable twice: it needs tools outside the course constraints (a voice service and access to a real mailbox, which would also expose personal data), and 160 hours do not fit into 132. The team rewrites it inside the scope as "By November 6, JARVIS logs e-mail triage from one command, offline", which is in fact Objective 3.
      

      The data decision. The team would like to use data from a family business. It has anonymised the rows, but it has neither the written permission of the organization nor the instructor's approval, so it starts with the default data set and keeps the request open.
      

      Where these deliverables go next. The objectives' dates are the due dates of Brick 3 (October 15), Brick 4 (October 22, end of Phase 1) and Brick 7 (the Alpha, November 6–12), and the January test is applied at the dress rehearsal (Class 14) and the Product Defense (Class 15). The hours you log on JARVIS from Class 5 onward become the setup cost in your economic model, as the Weekly Progress Report template asks.

      Slide 30 Demo 3 — the SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) scorer, statement by statement
      
 
      Demo 3 — SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objective scorer and project-selection rule
      Task of the code. Store five draft objectives as records, with one field for each letter of SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound); compute the weeks and hours available before each deadline, score the five letters with explicit rules, print a verdict per objective, and apply the project-selection rule (own data only with anonymisation, written permission and instructor approval).
      How it relates to the lecture. Lesson 3: scope and constraints (allowed tools, team capacity, the final date), SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound) objectives and the January test, and the project-selection rule. The objectives, their dates and the data decision are Brick 2 deliverables.
      
  
      The steps below are the real execution of demo3_smart_objectives.py, recorded statement by statement with Python 3. Keyboard: space = start/pause, ← → = one step.
      
 
      
  
  
  
  
 
      
 
      
  
      1. 1# =====================================================================
      2. 2# DEMO 3 - FIVE DRAFT OBJECTIVES, ONE JANUARY TEST
      3. 3# CS (Computer Science) 251 - Integrative Project 1 - Class 2, Lesson 3
      4. 4#
      5. 5# TASK OF THIS CODE: score five objectives drafted by a team against
      6. 6# the five SMART criteria (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant,
      7. 7# Time-bound). Each objective is stored as a record with one field per
      8. 8# letter; a letter is satisfied only when its field is filled and passes
      9. 9# an explicit rule (Achievable compares the hours needed with the team's
      10. 10# capacity and the tools the course allows; Time-bound applies the
      11. 11# "January test"). The program then checks whether the team may use
      12. 12# its own real data or must use the default data set.
      13. 13#
      14. 14# HOW IT RELATES TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 3 - scope, assumptions,
      15. 15# constraints, SMART objectives and project selection. The objectives
      16. 16# and the selection decision go into Brick 2; their dates are the
      17. 17# deadlines of Bricks 3, 4 and 7 and of the Product Defense.
      18. 18#
      19. 19# Standard library only - runs with Python 3.12 or newer.
      20. 20# Educational material - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub (c) 2026.
      21. 21# Use is subject to the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and
      22. 22# Acceptable Use Policy (v2.0):
      23. 23# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
      24. 24# =====================================================================
      25. 25 
      26. 26# Import the date type from the standard library to work with deadlines
      27. 27from datetime import date
      28. 28 
      29. 29# Today: the day of Class 2
      30. 30TODAY = date(2026, 10, 2)
      31. 31 
      32. 32# The Product Defense: every objective must be demonstrable on this day (the January test)
      33. 33FINAL = date(2027, 1, 22)
      34. 34 
      35. 35# The research questions accepted in Lesson 1; an objective is Relevant only if it serves one of them
      36. 36RQS = {"RQ1", "RQ2", "RQ3"}
      37. 37 
      38. 38# The tools allowed by the course constraints: Python standard library, one free API tier, GitHub
      39. 39ALLOWED = {"python", "csv", "statistics", "sqlite3", "free_api", "github"}
      40. 40 
      41. 41# Team capacity: 3 members x 4 hours per week (2 h workshop + 2 h at home)
      42. 42HOURS_PER_WEEK = 3 * 4
      43. 43 
      44. 44# The five draft objectives; None means the field is missing
      45. 45objectives = [
      46. 46    # Objective 1: the classic vague objective - no what, no measure, no estimate, no question, no date
      47. 47    {"id": 1, "what": None, "measure": None, "needs": {"python"}, "hours": None, "rq": None, "due": None},
      48. 48    # Objective 2: the statistics objective of Phase 1 (Brick 4 is due on October 22)
      49. 49    {"id": 2, "what": "14-day log + SD per routine", "measure": "SD of minutes per routine", "needs": {"python", "csv", "statistics"}, "hours": 10, "rq": "RQ1", "due": date(2026, 10, 22)},
      50. 50    # Objective 3: the first automation, shown at the Alpha demo on November 6
      51. 51    {"id": 3, "what": "e-mail triage logged by JARVIS offline", "measure": "minutes saved per run", "needs": {"python", "sqlite3"}, "hours": 24, "rq": "RQ3", "due": date(2026, 11, 6)},
      52. 52    # Objective 4: scope creep - voice, calendar and real e-mail access
      53. 53    {"id": 4, "what": "voice + calendar + e-mail assistant", "measure": "number of features", "needs": {"python", "voice_api", "email_account"}, "hours": 160, "rq": "RQ3", "due": date(2026, 12, 18)},
      54. 54    # Objective 5: the economics objective of Brick 3 (due October 15)
      55. 55    {"id": 5, "what": "break-even of the 20 $ paid tier", "measure": "break-even hours per month", "needs": {"python", "csv"}, "hours": 8, "rq": "RQ2", "due": date(2026, 10, 15)},
      56. 56# This closing bracket ends the list of objectives
      57. 57]
      58. 58 
      59. 59 
      60. 60# Define the function that scores one objective on the five letters
      61. 61def smart(obj):
      62. 62    # Whole weeks left before the deadline (0 when there is no deadline)
      63. 63    weeks = (obj["due"] - TODAY).days // 7 if obj["due"] else 0
      64. 64    # Hours the team can spend before the deadline
      65. 65    capacity = weeks * HOURS_PER_WEEK
      66. 66    # S: the objective names exactly what will be delivered
      67. 67    s = obj["what"] is not None
      68. 68    # M: the objective names how success will be measured
      69. 69    m = obj["measure"] is not None
      70. 70    # A: only allowed tools are needed, and the estimate fits inside the capacity
      71. 71    a = obj["needs"] <= ALLOWED and obj["hours"] is not None and obj["hours"] <= capacity
      72. 72    # R: the objective serves one of the accepted research questions
      73. 73    r = obj["rq"] in RQS
      74. 74    # T: the objective has a date, and the date passes the January test
      75. 75    t = obj["due"] is not None and obj["due"] <= FINAL
      76. 76    # Send back the five verdicts together with the capacity that was used
      77. 77    return {"S": s, "M": m, "A": a, "R": r, "T": t, "capacity": capacity}
      78. 78 
      79. 79 
      80. 80# Start an empty scorecard: objective number -> five verdicts
      81. 81scorecard = {}
      82. 82 
      83. 83# Score the objectives one at a time
      84. 84for obj in objectives:
      85. 85    # Apply the five rules to this objective
      86. 86    letters = smart(obj)
      87. 87    # Store the verdicts in the scorecard
      88. 88    scorecard[obj["id"]] = letters
      89. 89    # An objective is SMART only when all five letters are true
      90. 90    is_smart = all(letters[k] for k in "SMART")
      91. 91    # Build a compact view such as S+ M+ A- R+ T+
      92. 92    marks = " ".join(k + ("+" if letters[k] else "-") for k in "SMART")
      93. 93    # Print one line per objective: number, letters, verdict
      94. 94    print(f"Objective {obj['id']}: {marks} -> {'SMART' if is_smart else 'rewrite'} (capacity {letters['capacity']} h)")
      95. 95 
      96. 96# The team's proposal for its data: its own real data from a family business
      97. 97proposal = {"own_data": True, "no_names": True, "no_message_contents": True, "written_permission": False, "instructor_approved": False}
      98. 98 
      99. 99# The selection rule: own data only when every protection is in place
      100. 100if proposal["own_data"] and all(proposal[k] for k in ("no_names", "no_message_contents", "written_permission", "instructor_approved")):
      101. 101    # Every condition is met: the team may use its own data
      102. 102    decision = "own data approved"
      103. 103# Otherwise the team works with the synthetic default data set
      104. 104else:
      105. 105    # The default data set is always allowed
      106. 106    decision = "default data set: boreal_routines_2026.csv"
      107. 107 
      108. 108# Print the decision that goes into Brick 2
      109. 109print("DATA DECISION:", decision)
      110. 110

        How the code works — step by step
        1. Press Start. The constants are stored first: TODAY (the day of Class 2), FINAL (the Product Defense), the accepted research questions RQS, the allowed tools ALLOWED, and the capacity HOURS_PER_WEEK = 3 × 4 = 12.
        2. The list objectives is built in one step. Each objective is a dictionary; a missing field holds None. The scorecard grid on the right shows five empty rows.
        3. The loop takes Objective 1 and calls smart(). Inside the function, weeks is 0 because there is no due date, so capacity is 0.
        4. Each letter is one statement. For Objective 1 every result is False: what and measure are None, the hours were never estimated, there is no research question and no date. Five red cells appear.
        5. Objective 2: October 22 is 20 days after today, so weeks = 20 // 7 = 2 and capacity = 24 hours. The needs {python, csv, statistics} are a subset of ALLOWED (the operator <= on sets tests is a subset of), and 10 ≤ 24. All five cells turn green.
        6. Objective 4: the needs include voice_api and email_account, which are not allowed, and 160 hours exceed the capacity of 132. Only cell A turns red. This is the typical pattern of scope creep: specific, measurable, relevant and dated, but not achievable.
        7. The timeline under the grid places every deadline on the course calendar, next to the Brick dates, the Alpha, the Mid-Term and the Product Defense.
        8. Finally the program reads the team's data proposal. all(...) is false because written permission and approval are missing, so the else branch runs and decision becomes the default data set.
        9. Pause, Next step, Back and the clickable Execution log let you stop on any letter of any objective and ask the class: true or false, and why?

        Why we cite (0:45–0:46)
        Slide 34 Why we cite — and where credible sources come from
        

        A reference identifies a source precisely enough for a reader to find it; a citation is the short pointer in your text that sends the reader to that reference. Citation has two purposes: it lets your reader verify a claim, and it gives credit to the work you build on. In this course you cite four kinds of material: the books and articles you use, the documentation pages of the functions you call, the code you reuse, and any AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance you receive. That rule is in the course's Brick rules, in section 18 of the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy and in the University's academic-honesty policy.
        


        Where to find credible sources (0:46–0:48)
        Still on slideSlide 34 — Why we cite — and where credible sources come from
        

          

        • Textbooks and scholarly books. Leedy and Ormrod (2019) for the research process; for the refreshers, a microeconomics and a statistics textbook. OpenStax, a non-profit of Rice University, publishes both free and peer-reviewed.
          • 

        • Scholarly articles. Library databases and Google Scholar. In Québec, BAnQ (Bibliothèque et Archives nationales du Québec) gives every resident a free subscription with access to many databases.
          • 

        • Official documentation. The Python documentation for statistics, csv, sqlite3 and datetime; the API (Application Programming Interface) provider's own pages for its quotas, read on a given date and cited with that date.
          • 

        • Official statistics. Agencies such as Statistics Canada for definitions and published figures.
          • 

        

        Slide 35 The CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) test — five questions for any source
        To judge any source, apply the CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) test, published by the librarian Sarah Blakeslee in 2004. Currency: when was it published or updated? Relevance: does it answer my question? Authority: who wrote it, and what qualifies them? Accuracy: is there evidence, are there references, can it be checked? Purpose: does it inform, sell or persuade? An anonymous blog post that sells a productivity course fails Authority, Accuracy and Purpose even when its advice sounds right. Wikipedia is useful to find the primary sources it cites: read those and cite them instead.
        

        APA (American Psychological Association) 7 in one pattern (0:48–0:49)
        Slide 36 APA (American Psychological Association) 7 in one pattern
        

        The course uses the 7th edition of the Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association, presented on the official APA (American Psychological Association) Style site. Every reference follows one pattern: Author. (Date). Title. Source.
        

          

        • Book: Leedy, P. D., & Ormrod, J. E. (2019). Practical research: Planning and design (12th ed.). Pearson Education.
          • 

        • Documentation page whose content changes and has no date: Python Software Foundation. (n.d.). statistics — Mathematical statistics functions. Python documentation. Retrieved October 1, 2026, from https://docs.python.org/3/library/statistics.html
          • 

        • Software or code: Author. (Year). Title (Version) [Computer software]. Publisher. URL (Uniform Resource Locator)
          • 

        • AI (Artificial Intelligence) assistance: APA (American Psychological Association)'s blog gives the pattern Company. (Year). Name of the tool (version) [Large language model]. URL (Uniform Resource Locator).
          • 

        

        In the text, write (Leedy & Ormrod, 2019), or Leedy and Ormrod (2019) state that...; with three or more authors, (Shapiro et al., 2022). The reference list is sorted alphabetically by the first author's surname. A DOI (Digital Object Identifier) is a permanent identifier printed as https://doi.org/...; it replaces the URL (Uniform Resource Locator) when the source has one.
        

        Finding one expert (0:49–0:50)
        Slide 37 Finding one expert
        

        An expert, for Brick 2, is a person with direct experience of the problem: a small-business owner, an office manager, a statistics tutor, an industry contact. Write a short message: who you are, the purpose, a time limit of 20 minutes, three open questions linked to your research questions, a request for permission to take notes, and how you will anonymise the answers (the job title appears in the report, not the name, unless the expert agrees in writing). Example questions, one per research question. For RQ1 (Research Question 1): "Which routine takes the most time in your office, and how do you know?" For RQ2 (Research Question 2): "How do you decide whether a software subscription is worth its price?" For RQ3 (Research Question 3), the risk: "What would make you stop using an assistant after one week?"

        Task of the example. Evaluate five candidate sources for the JARVIS project with the CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) test, keep the credible ones, format each kept source as an APA (American Psychological Association) 7 reference, build its in-text citation, and sort the reference list alphabetically by first author.
        How it relates to this lesson. This is Lesson 4 applied: where to find credible sources, how to judge them, and the APA (American Psychological Association) 7 pattern Author. (Date). Title. Source. The demo performs each step in Python; the figure shows the anatomy of a reference.
        The candidates. After the workshop the team has five candidate sources: the course textbook by Leedy and Ormrod; the OpenStax Principles of Microeconomics; the OpenStax Introductory Statistics; the Python documentation page of the statistics module; and a blog post titled "10 AI (Artificial Intelligence) hacks that save 5 hours a day", with no author and no date, that ends with an offer for a paid course.
        

        The test. The three textbooks and the documentation page pass all five CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) questions. The blog post passes only Relevance: it has no date (Currency), no identifiable author (Authority), no evidence or references (Accuracy), and it is written to sell (Purpose). It is set aside; if one of its ideas is useful, the team looks for a credible source that supports it.
        

        The list. The four kept sources are formatted in APA (American Psychological Association) 7 and sorted: Illowsky & Dean (2023); Leedy & Ormrod (2019); Python Software Foundation (n.d.); Shapiro et al. (2022). Brick 2 asks for at least five sources, so the team adds a fifth one at home, for example the documentation page of the free API (Application Programming Interface) tier it plans to use, read and cited with the date.

The textbooks become the citations for every formula in Brick 3 (economics) and Brick 4 (statistics), and the statistics documentation states the n − 1 rule you will test in Brick 6. The list grows into the References section of the report skeleton (Brick 9) and of the full draft (Brick 12). The expert is a natural guest for the public Product Defense on January 22.

        42. 42# Define the function that formats a book in APA 7: Author. (Year). *Title* (edition). Publisher. URL
        43. 43def apa_book(s):
        44. 44    # Build the reference; the asterisks mark the italic title, as in Markdown
        45. 45    ref = f"{s['author']} ({s['year']}). *{s['title']}* ({s['edition']}). {s['publisher']}."
        46. 46    # Add the address only when the book is online
        47. 47    return ref + (f" {s['url']}" if s["url"] else "")
        48. 48

        50. 50# Define the function that formats a web page whose content changes, with its retrieval date
        51. 51def apa_web(s):
        52. 52    # An organization written as author is followed by a period, like a person's name
        53. 53    return f"{s['author']}. ({s['year']}). *{s['title']}*. {s['site']}. Retrieved {s['retrieved']}, from {s['url']}"

        55. 55 
        56. 56# Define the function that builds the parenthetical in-text citation
        57. 57def in_text(s):
        58. 58    # Count the authors
        59. 59    n = len(s["surnames"])
        60. 60    # One author: the surname or the organization name
        61. 61    if n == 1:
        62. 62        # For example (Python Software Foundation, n.d.)
        63. 63        names = s["surnames"][0]
        64. 64    # Two authors: both surnames joined by an ampersand
        65. 65    elif n == 2:
        66. 66        # For example (Leedy & Ormrod, 2019)
        67. 67        names = f"{s['surnames'][0]} & {s['surnames'][1]}"
        68. 68    # Three or more authors: the first surname followed by et al.
        69. 69    else:
        70. 70        # For example (Shapiro et al., 2022)
        71. 71        names = f"{s['surnames'][0]} et al."
        72. 72    # Send back the citation with the year
        73. 73    return f"({names}, {s['year']})"

        84. 84    # Count how many of the five CRAAP questions the source passes
        85. 85    score = sum(s[c] for c in CRITERIA)

        87. 87    if score == 5:

        89. 89        ref = apa_book(s) if s["type"] == "book" else apa_web(s)

        91. 91        reference_list.append((ref, in_text(s)))

        Execution log — every step that has run (click a line to return to it)
          

          How the code works — step by step
          1. Press Start. CRITERIA holds the five CRAAP (Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose) questions; the list sources is built in one step — five dictionaries, each with the bibliographic fields and one true/false answer per question. Five rows of five empty boxes appear.
          2. Three functions are defined: apa_book(), apa_web() and in_text(). Defining them runs nothing; watch the log: the next steps happen in the loop.
          3. For each source, score = sum(...) adds the five answers — in Python, True counts as 1 and False as 0. The five boxes of the row fill in green or red.
          4. The textbook by Leedy and Ormrod scores 5/5. apa_book() builds the reference; the asterisks around the title mark italics, exactly as in Markdown. in_text() sees two surnames and returns (Leedy & Ormrod, 2019).
          5. The OpenStax microeconomics book has three authors, so in_text() takes the else branch and returns (Shapiro et al., 2022).
          6. The documentation page is a web page whose content changes: apa_web() adds Retrieved October 1, 2026, from and the address, and the organization stands in place of a person as author.
          7. The blog post scores 1/5. The else branch stores it in rejected and prints the failed criteria, computed with a list comprehension.
          8. After the loop, reference_list.sort(...) orders the references alphabetically, as APA (American Psychological Association) 7 requires; the panel Reference list redraws in the new order with hanging indents.
          9. Pause on the scoring of the blog post and ask the class: which other criterion would you add for code you copy from a forum?

          Lesson 5 — The data dictionary and personal data
          Every column's meaning, Python type and unit — what could be wrong with it — and why a time log is personal information.
          Slide 41 Lesson 5 — The data dictionary and personal data
          Lecture notes
          0:50–0:56
          What a data dictionary is (0:50–0:51)
          Slide 42 What a data dictionary is
          

          A data dictionary is a table that documents every column of a data set: its name, its meaning, its data type, its unit or format, the allowed values, an example, and what could be wrong with it. It states the rules that both the people who collect the data and the code that reads it must follow. Brick 2 asks for the dictionary of boreal_routines_2026.csv (nine columns) with one more column, possible issue, filled in for every row.
          

          Python types for each column (0:51–0:53)
          Slide 43 Python types for each column
          

          When Python reads a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file, every value arrives as text, of type str. The loader you will write in Brick 5 converts each value to its proper type. The type of a value decides which operations are allowed on it: you can add two integers, but not two dates.
          

          


          
Column
Python type
Conversion

          
          


          
date
datetime.date
date.fromisoformat("2026-09-07")

          

          
staff_id, routine, category, tool
str (text)
none — already text

          

          
start_hour, minutes, interruptions
int (integer)
int("42")

          

          
done
bool (Boolean: True or False), stored as 0/1
row["done"] == "1"

          
          

          

          Two traps. int("25 min") raises a ValueError: the unit belongs in the dictionary, not in the cell. And bool("0") is True, because Python treats every non-empty text as true. Never convert done with bool(). The type float (a number with decimals) appears later, when you compute an average or a cost in dollars.
          

          What could be wrong with it (0:53–0:55)
          Slide 44 What could be wrong — four checks of individual values
          

          For every column, the dictionary records the possible issues. Data-quality work commonly checks four properties of individual values:
          

            

          • Completeness: a value is present; an empty minutes cell fails.
            • 

          • Validity: a value has the right type, format and range, which fails for -5 minutes, 25 min, a date typed 08/09/2026, a start hour of 27.
            • 

          • Consistency: a value agrees with the agreed list and with the rest of the data, which fails for emial_triage instead of email_triage; Manual written with a capital letter while every other row says manual.
            • 

          • Uniqueness: each run is recorded once; two identical rows double the minutes.
            • 

          

          These checks become code later in the course. The loader skips and counts bad rows instead of crashing (Brick 5). The database refuses negative minutes and duplicates with a CHECK and a UNIQUE constraint (Brick 6). Sprint 1 must demonstrate three bad-input cases (Brick 10).
          

          A time log is personal data (0:55–0:56)
          Slide 45 A time log is personal data
          

          Personal information is information about an identifiable individual. That is the definition used by PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), Canada's federal privacy law for the private sector, explained by the OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada). Québec's private-sector act, as amended by Law 25 and supervised by the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec), uses a similar definition: information about a natural person that allows that person to be identified, directly or indirectly. A time log says when a person worked, on what, for how long and how often they were interrupted. It is personal information.
          

          Two words are often confused. De-identified information no longer identifies a person directly (a code such as S3 replaces the name), but it can still be linked back to the person. Anonymized information can never be linked back to a person, directly or indirectly, and the operation is irreversible. Our staff codes are de-identification, so the data stays private.
          

          The privacy risks of our project: a real name typed where a code is expected; message contents in a free-text column; small groups (with five staff, a chart per person identifies the person); and public repositories. The mitigations: codes instead of names; no message contents, ever; raw logs only in the private team repository; dashboards that show aggregated numbers per routine, never per person. See section 6.7, section 8.3 and section 20 of the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and Acceptable Use Policy. This is general information, not legal advice (section 16).
          Key terms of this lesson
          TermScientific explanation
          Data dictionaryA table that documents every column of a data set: name, meaning, type, unit or format, allowed values, example and possible issues.
          Data typeThe kind of value — str, int, float, bool, datetime.date — which decides the operations allowed on it.
          Type conversionTurning text read from a file into the proper type, for example int("42") or date.fromisoformat("2026-09-07").
          Completeness / validity / consistency / uniquenessFour checks of individual values: present; right type, format and range; agrees with the agreed list; recorded once.
          Personal informationInformation about an identifiable individual, as PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) defines it; in Québec, information that allows a person to be identified directly or indirectly.
          De-identifiedNo direct identifier (a code replaces the name), but the data can still be linked back — it remains personal information.
          AnonymizedCan never be linked back to a person, directly or indirectly; the operation is irreversible.
          Aggregated dataNumbers computed over a group (for example, mean minutes per routine) instead of rows about one person.

          What the dictionary finds. Row 1 is correct. Row 2 fails completeness. Rows 3 and 4 fail validity (a negative duration; a date that is not yyyy-mm-dd). Row 5 repeats row 1 (uniqueness). Row 6 fails consistency (a routine name that is not on the list). Row 7 has four problems: a name instead of a code and a free-text column with message contents (two privacy risks), an hour outside 0–23 and a unit inside the value (two validity problems). Total: nine problems in seven rows. The names Julie Roy and Lavoie are fictional.
          

          What the team decides. Rows 2–7 are returned to their authors for correction. The team writes three data-quality risks and one privacy risk, each with its mitigation, in Brick 2, for example: "Risk: a staff member types their name in staff_id. Mitigation: the loader accepts only S1–S5 and rejects the row; the codes table is never committed."

          • The privacy rules apply to every Brick and to the dashboard of Brick 11, which may show aggregated numbers only. Personal time logs are ignored by Git (data/timelog_*.csv in .gitignore).
