          Demo 5 — Data-dictionary validator with privacy checks
          Task of the code. Validate seven rows against a five-column data dictionary: convert dates with date.fromisoformat and minutes with int(), check codes with a regular expression and routines against the agreed list, detect a duplicate run with a set of keys, flag undocumented columns as a privacy risk, and count the problems per data-quality property.
          How it relates to the lecture. Lesson 5: the data dictionary with Python types, completeness / validity / consistency / uniqueness, and personal information. The rules are the specification of the loader (Brick 5), of the database constraints (Brick 6) and of the validation tests (Brick 10).
          
  
          The steps below are the real execution of demo5_data_dictionary.py, recorded statement by statement with Python 3. Keyboard: space = start/pause, ← → = one step.
          
 
          
  
  
  
  
 
          
 
          
  
          1. 1# =====================================================================
          2. 2# DEMO 5 - SEVEN ROWS, ONE DATA DICTIONARY
          3. 3# CS (Computer Science) 251 - Integrative Project 1 - Class 2, Lesson 5
          4. 4#
          5. 5# TASK OF THIS CODE: before anyone writes the loader, check seven rows
          6. 6# received from the staff against the data dictionary. Every value is
          7. 7# converted to its Python type; every problem is classified by data-
          8. 8# quality dimension (completeness, validity, consistency, uniqueness);
          9. 9# privacy risks are flagged (a real name where an anonymous code is
          10. 10# expected, a column that holds message contents). The program ends
          11. 11# with a count of problems per dimension.
          12. 12#
          13. 13# HOW IT RELATES TO THE LECTURE: Lesson 5 - the data dictionary with
          14. 14# Python types, "what could be wrong with it", and the time log as
          15. 15# personal data. The dictionary and the risks are Brick 2 deliverables;
          16. 16# the same rules become the loader of Brick 5, the database constraints
          17. 17# of Brick 6 and the input-validation tests of Brick 10.
          18. 18#
          19. 19# Standard library only - runs with Python 3.12 or newer.
          20. 20# Educational material - Cyber.SoHo Educational Hub (c) 2026.
          21. 21# Use is subject to the Cyber.SoHo Legal Notice, Terms of Use and
          22. 22# Acceptable Use Policy (v2.0):
          23. 23# https://cyber-soho.github.io/prevmon/00.01.%20cyber.soho%20-%20legal.html
          24. 24# =====================================================================
          25. 25 
          26. 26# Import the date type: it converts text such as "2026-09-08" into a real calendar date
          27. 27from datetime import date
          28. 28 
          29. 29# Import the module for regular expressions, used to check the format of the staff code
          30. 30import re
          31. 31 
          32. 32# Import Counter, a dictionary that counts things, from the standard collections module
          33. 33from collections import Counter
          34. 34 
          35. 35# The data dictionary (five of the nine columns): column -> (Python type, rule)
          36. 36DICTIONARY = {
          37. 37    # The day of the run, written year-month-day
          38. 38    "date": ("datetime.date", "yyyy-mm-dd, a real calendar day"),
          39. 39    # An anonymous code for the person - never a name
          40. 40    "staff_id": ("str", "S1 to S5"),
          41. 41    # The name of the routine, from the agreed list of six
          42. 42    "routine": ("str", "one of the six routines"),
          43. 43    # The hour the run started, on a 24-hour clock
          44. 44    "start_hour": ("int", "0 to 23"),
          45. 45    # The duration of the run in minutes, digits only
          46. 46    "minutes": ("int", "0 or more"),
          47. 47# This closing brace ends the data dictionary
          48. 48}
          49. 49 
          50. 50# The agreed list of the six routines of Boréal Studio
          51. 51ROUTINES = {"email_triage", "daily_report", "scheduling", "invoice_check", "standup_notes", "social_post"}
          52. 52 
          53. 53# The format of an anonymous staff code: the letter S followed by a digit from 1 to 5
          54. 54STAFF = re.compile(r"S[1-5]")
          55. 55 
          56. 56# Seven rows as they arrived (every value is text, exactly as a CSV file delivers it)
          57. 57rows = [
          58. 58    # Row 1: a correct row
          59. 59    {"date": "2026-09-08", "staff_id": "S1", "routine": "email_triage", "start_hour": "8", "minutes": "41"},
          60. 60    # Row 2: the minutes cell is empty
          61. 61    {"date": "2026-09-08", "staff_id": "S2", "routine": "daily_report", "start_hour": "17", "minutes": ""},
          62. 62    # Row 3: a negative duration
          63. 63    {"date": "2026-09-08", "staff_id": "S3", "routine": "invoice_check", "start_hour": "14", "minutes": "-5"},
          64. 64    # Row 4: the date typed day/month/year instead of year-month-day
          65. 65    {"date": "08/09/2026", "staff_id": "S4", "routine": "scheduling", "start_hour": "10", "minutes": "15"},
          66. 66    # Row 5: the same run as row 1, recorded a second time
          67. 67    {"date": "2026-09-08", "staff_id": "S1", "routine": "email_triage", "start_hour": "8", "minutes": "41"},
          68. 68    # Row 6: a typing error in the routine name
          69. 69    {"date": "2026-09-08", "staff_id": "S5", "routine": "emial_triage", "start_hour": "9", "minutes": "37"},
          70. 70    # Row 7: a real name, an impossible hour, a unit inside the value, and an extra column with message contents
          71. 71    {"date": "2026-09-08", "staff_id": "Julie Roy", "routine": "social_post", "start_hour": "27", "minutes": "25 min", "note": "Re: Lavoie invoice - client unhappy"},
          72. 72# This closing bracket ends the list of rows
          73. 73]
          74. 74 
          75. 75 
          76. 76# Define the function that checks one row against the dictionary and returns its problems
          77. 77def validate(row):
          78. 78    # Start with no problems: column -> "dimension: explanation"
          79. 79    problems = {}
          80. 80    # Try to convert the date text into a real date
          81. 81    try:
          82. 82        # fromisoformat accepts only the yyyy-mm-dd form
          83. 83        date.fromisoformat(row["date"])
          84. 84    # The conversion fails when the text does not follow the format
          85. 85    except ValueError:
          86. 86        # Record a validity problem for this column
          87. 87        problems["date"] = "validity: not yyyy-mm-dd"
          88. 88    # The staff code must match the anonymous format exactly
          89. 89    if not STAFF.fullmatch(row["staff_id"]):
          90. 90        # Anything else could identify a person
          91. 91        problems["staff_id"] = "privacy: not an anonymous code"
          92. 92    # The routine must belong to the agreed list
          93. 93    if row["routine"] not in ROUTINES:
          94. 94        # A value outside the list disagrees with the rest of the data
          95. 95        problems["routine"] = "consistency: unknown routine"
          96. 96    # The hour must be digits and lie between 0 and 23
          97. 97    if not row["start_hour"].isdigit() or not 0 <= int(row["start_hour"]) <= 23:
          98. 98        # Record a validity problem for the hour
          99. 99        problems["start_hour"] = "validity: outside 0-23"
          100. 100    # An empty cell means the value is missing
          101. 101    if row["minutes"] == "":
          102. 102        # Record a completeness problem
          103. 103        problems["minutes"] = "completeness: missing value"
          104. 104    # Otherwise the text must convert to an integer that is not negative
          105. 105    else:
          106. 106        # Try the conversion that the loader will do
          107. 107        try:
          108. 108            # int() accepts digits with an optional sign, nothing else
          109. 109            minutes = int(row["minutes"])
          110. 110            # A duration can never be below zero
          111. 111            if minutes < 0:
          112. 112                # Record a validity problem for the negative value
          113. 113                problems["minutes"] = "validity: negative duration"
          114. 114        # Text such as "25 min" cannot become an integer
          115. 115        except ValueError:
          116. 116            # Record a validity problem for the format
          117. 117            problems["minutes"] = "validity: not an integer"
          118. 118    # Any column that is not in the dictionary must not be stored
          119. 119    for column in row:
          120. 120        # Compare each column name with the dictionary
          121. 121        if column not in DICTIONARY:
          122. 122            # An undocumented free-text column may hold message contents
          123. 123            problems[column] = "privacy: column not in the dictionary"
          124. 124    # Send back all the problems found in this row
          125. 125    return problems
          126. 126 
          127. 127 
          128. 128# The identity of a run: the same four values twice means the same run was recorded twice
          129. 129seen = set()
          130. 130 
          131. 131# The report: row number -> problems found in that row
          132. 132report = {}
          133. 133 
          134. 134# Check the rows one at a time, numbering them from 1
          135. 135for number, row in enumerate(rows, start=1):
          136. 136    # Apply every rule of the dictionary to this row
          137. 137    problems = validate(row)
          138. 138    # Build the identity of the run from the four values that define it
          139. 139    key = (row["date"], row["staff_id"], row["routine"], row["start_hour"])
          140. 140    # A key that was already seen is a duplicate
          141. 141    if key in seen:
          142. 142        # Record a uniqueness problem for the whole row
          143. 143        problems["row"] = "uniqueness: duplicate of an earlier row"
          144. 144    # Remember this key for the rows that follow
          145. 145    seen.add(key)
          146. 146    # Store the problems of this row in the report
          147. 147    report[number] = problems
          148. 148    # Print the row number and its problems (OK when there are none)
          149. 149    print(f"row {number}: {problems if problems else 'OK'}")
          150. 150 
          151. 151# Count the problems per dimension, using the word before the colon
          152. 152counts = Counter(message.split(":")[0] for found in report.values() for message in found.values())
          153. 153 
          154. 154# Print the counts: this is the data-quality and privacy summary of Brick 2
          155. 155print("PROBLEMS PER DIMENSION:", dict(counts))
          156. 156

            How the code works — step by step
            1. Press Start. Three imports: date for the date conversion, re for the code format, Counter to count problems. Then DICTIONARY is built: five columns, each with its Python type and its rule.
            2. ROUTINES is a set — the agreed list of six routines; STAFF is a regular expression meaning the letter S followed by a digit from 1 to 5. rows holds the seven rows as text, exactly as a CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file delivers them.
            3. def validate(...) defines the checks. The loop takes row 1 and calls validate(). The matrix on the right highlights row 1; every cell turns green because no rule fails.
            4. Row 2: the minutes cell is empty, so the branch if row["minutes"] == "" records a completeness problem. Note the order of the checks: an empty cell is tested before the conversion, so it is reported as missing, not as invalid.
            5. Row 4: date.fromisoformat("08/09/2026") raises a ValueError — the execution log shows the exception, and the next step is the except line, which records a validity problem. This is exactly how the loader of Brick 5 will survive a bad row instead of crashing.
            6. Row 5 passes validate(), but its key (date, staff_id, routine, start_hour) is already in the set seen: the row is a duplicate — uniqueness. The same four columns form the UNIQUE constraint of the database in Brick 6.
            7. Row 7 collects four problems: STAFF.fullmatch("Julie Roy") returns None (privacy); 27 is outside 0–23 (validity); int("25 min") raises ValueError (validity); and the column note is not in the dictionary (privacy — message contents).
            8. After the loop, Counter(...) counts the problems by the word before the colon. The bar chart shows completeness 1, validity 4, consistency 1, uniqueness 1, privacy 2.
            9. Pause on row 7 and ask: which of these four problems would also be a privacy incident if the file were pushed to a public repository?

            click a card to turn it
            Slide 49 Remember — Lesson 5
            Card 1 of 5
            What does a data dictionary contain?
            Click to see the answer
            Answer
            For every column: name, meaning, data type, unit or format, allowed values, an example, and what could be wrong with it.
            Card 2 of 5
            Python type of date, minutes, routine and done?
            Click to see the answer
            Answer
            date → datetime.date; minutes → int; routine → str; done → bool, stored as 0/1 and converted with row["done"] == "1".
            Card 3 of 5
            Why does int("25 min") fail?
            Click to see the answer
            Answer
            int() accepts only digits with an optional sign; the text contains a unit, so Python raises ValueError. Units belong in the dictionary, not in the cell.
            Card 4 of 5
            The four checks of individual values?
            Click to see the answer
            Answer
            Completeness (present), validity (type, format, range), consistency (agrees with the agreed list), uniqueness (recorded once).
            Card 5 of 5
            De-identified or anonymized?
            Click to see the answer
            Answer
            De-identified: a code replaces the name but the data can be linked back — still personal information. Anonymized: can never be linked back, irreversibly.

            • What it is. One file in your team repository, docs/requirements.md, that turns today's five lessons into your project's first formal document.

A problem statement of at most 150 words and three research questions (Lesson 1); five user stories with acceptance criteria — at least one for the owner, one for a staff member and one for "JARVIS with no API (Application Programming Interface) key" (Lesson 2); a data dictionary with at least three data-quality risks and one privacy risk with its mitigation (Lesson 5); a reference list of at least five credible sources in APA (American Psychological Association) 7, one expert and three interview questions (Lesson 4). Teams that propose their own data ask for approval in the workshop (Lesson 3).
